before: Objects can offer the same action while performing it differently. An interface is the set of actions a caller expects an object to support. If two delivery objects both have a process method, a single function can call that method without needing to know which kind of delivery it received. The object's own method supplies its specific behavior.

This style is often called duck typing: code cares whether the needed method exists, rather than requiring one particular class name or parent class. A class defines methods; an instance is an object created by calling the class. A method's first parameter self receives that instance automatically. A shared name does not mean the methods must return the same message.

Follow the returned value through the call. The outer function receives an object in its parameter. A dot selects its method, and the empty parentheses call that method. The method returns a string. The outer function returns that string to its own caller. Finally print displays it. Merely calling announce without returning its result from send_notice would make send_notice return None instead.

Process_delivery(item) should call and return item.process(). No common parent class is needed for that interface. This is one form of polymorphism: one calling operation can produce different appropriate behavior depending on the object.

Two objects can offer the same action but do it differently. Our shared function asks an object to send a notice. A bell rings. A light flashes.

The actions code expects an object to have are called its interface. Here, the needed action is `announce()`.

Our function only needs the object to have the right method. It does not need a certain class name or a shared parent class. This is called duck typing.

Both objects have an `announce` method, but each method can return a different message. When we call the method, `self` refers to that object.

Follow the message back through the calls. `send_notice` receives an object as `notice`. The dot in `notice.announce()` selects its method, and `()` runs it.

That method returns a message. `send_notice` returns the same message, and `print` shows it.

Without `return` in `send_notice`, that function would give back `None` instead.

For your delivery project, give both `BikeDelivery` and `LockerDelivery` a `process(self)` method.

The bike method returns `"Rider takes parcel"`. The locker method returns `"Parcel goes to locker"`.

In `process_delivery(item)`, call `item.process()` and return its result. The classes do not need a shared parent. Using the same action name for different behavior is called polymorphism.

Keep each delivery's work in its own method. Let the shared function call that method. Try both objects and check their messages.

The separate math question uses an inclusive range from 0 through 10. Inclusive means both ends count, so 10 is allowed.
